title: By tens
hookLine: ten questions asked at every number, from one to ten
carry: what helps, what to let go

lines: BESIDE A LOTUS POND IN CHAMPA.
cards: Any good mechanic has a checklist, even if it's only in their head. What's working? What needs attention?
What has to come out? What would make this run better? Ask the same few questions of every part, and nothing gets missed.
The thirty-fourth discourse, the last of the long ones, is built like that. Sariputta is speaking again, beside a lotus pond near the city of Champa.
And instead of one list per number, he asks the same ten questions at every number, one through ten.

teach.b: It's the Dasuttara Sutta, roughly, going up to ten. Here's how it works.

teach.h: WHAT HELPS, WHAT TO GROW, WHAT TO DROP
teach.b: At number one, Sariputta asks: what one thing helps most? Diligence, care in doing good. What one thing should be developed?
Mindfulness of the body, with gladness. What one thing should be fully understood? Contact, the meeting of the senses and the world, the kind that feeds clinging.
What one thing should be let go? The conceit I am. What leads to decline?
Careless attention. What leads to growth? Wise attention.
And so on, ten questions in all, down to: what one thing should be realized? A freedom of mind that can't be shaken.

teach.h: THEN ALL TEN AGAIN AT TWO, AND UP
teach.b: Then he goes to two and asks all ten questions again, with two things for each answer.
Then three, all the way to ten. Picture a grid: ten numbers down the side, ten questions across the top, every square filled.
A whole way of life folded into a table. And the questions are practical. Not what's true about the universe, but what helps, what to grow, what to drop, what's slipping, what's getting better.
Decline and growth often turn on the same thing done two ways: careless attention or wise attention.
The Long Discourses end here, not with a story or a death scene, but with a teacher handing the community a tool to check itself, number by number.

how: Many Buddhists learn the teaching through numbered lists, such as the four noble truths, the five precepts and the eightfold path, and monastic study in many countries still includes memorizing them.

o: counted up, one number at a time to ten
a tax of one part in ten for the temple
ten rules every monk must keep daily

games.q: number one in DN 34: tap the pairs.
p: the one thing that helps most
the one thing to let go

s: DN 34 is the last discourse in the Long Discourses
the collection of thirty-four ends with Sariputta's ten-by-ten grid.
each number in DN 34 gets only one list
each number gets the same ten questions: what helps, what to develop, what to let go, and more.
Sariputta speaks it, beside a lotus pond near Champa.

games.q: you're checking on your own life using Sariputta's questions. one thing leads to decline, one to growth. what's the difference?
games.why: at number one, decline comes from careless attention and growth from wise attention: the same mind, used two ways.

practice: Let the breath settle, then name ten good things in your life right now, one finger at a time; small is fine, a warm cup, a friend's message, working knees, a window, a song. Let each one land before the next.
When your hands are full, rest them in your lap and breathe with all ten.

wordCard.voice: By tens. Sariputta's last long discourse: ten questions, what helps, what to grow, what to let go, asked again at every number from one to ten. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dasuttara: going up to ten. the name of DN 34.

carryVoice: Your line: what helps, what to let go. Two questions that fit any day. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 34, Dasuttara Sutta (going up to ten)
